items.title: Expressions and equations
items.content: An expression has no equality sign; an equation states two expressions are equal. Like terms have identical variable parts. Use inverse operations while maintaining equality.

items.title: Distributive property
items.content: \(a(b+c)=ab+ac\). To solve \(ax+b=c\), isolate the variable: subtract \(b\), then divide by nonzero \(a\).

items.title: Exam checks
items.content:
Keep the equation balanced by doing the same operation to both sides.
Substitute the solution back into the original equation.

items.title: Variables, coefficients and terms
items.content: In \(5x-3y+7\), coefficients are 5 and -3; the constant is 7. Worked example: at \(x=2,y=1\), value is \(10-3+7=14\).

items.title: Combining like terms
items.content: Only terms with the same variable powers combine. Worked example: \(4x+3-2x+5=2x+8\).

items.title: Substitution
items.content: Insert the signed value with brackets. Worked example: for \(x=-2\), \(x^2-3x=4+6=10\).

items.title: Distributive property and simplification
items.content: Worked example: \(3(2x-5)+4x=6x-15+4x=10x-15\).

items.title: Solving a linear equation
items.content: Worked example: \(3x+7=22\). Subtract 7: \(3x=15\); divide by 3: \(x=5\). Check in the original equation.

items.title: Translating words into algebra
items.content: Let the unknown be a variable, translate one relation at a time. Worked example: “five more than twice a number is 19” gives \(2x+5=19\), so \(x=7\).

items.title: Simple formulas and rearrangement
items.content: Use inverse operations to isolate a requested variable. Worked example: from \(v=u+at\), solve for \(t\): \(t=(v-u)/a\), provided \(a\ne0\).

items.title: Simplify an expression
items.content: Collect like terms and preserve signs. Worked example: \(7a-3+2a+8=9a+5\).

items.title: Evaluate after substitution
items.content: Worked example: \(2x^2-y\) for \(x=3,y=4\) equals \(18-4=14\).

items.title: Solve a one-variable equation
items.content: Worked example: \(5(x-2)=20\); divide by 5, add 2: \(x=6\).

items.title: Form an equation from a statement
items.content: Worked example: a number decreased by 8 is 13: \(x-8=13\), hence \(x=21\).

items.title: Find and correct an error
items.content: Substitute a proposed solution into both sides. If they differ, revisit the inverse-operation step. Worked example: the claim x = 3 solves 2x + 3 = 11 fails because 9 ≠ 11; solving gives x = 4.

items.title: Why the distributive property works
items.content: Multiplication over addition means \(a(b+c)=ab+ac\): combine \(a\) copies of each addend, or use the area of a rectangle split into widths \(b\) and \(c\).

items.title: Why equation operations preserve solutions
items.content: Adding or subtracting the same quantity from both sides preserves equality. Dividing or multiplying both sides by the same nonzero number also preserves it.

items.title: Why like terms combine
items.content: Like terms count the same unit: \(3x+2x\) is three x-units plus two x-units, or \(5x\); \(x\) and \(x^2\) are different units.

sections.title: Common errors and how to avoid them

items.title: Combining unlike terms
items.content: Do not combine \(x\) with \(x^2\) or a constant.

items.title: Sign error after subtraction
items.content: Subtract the whole term from both sides; use parentheses when necessary.

items.title: Applying multiplication to only one term
items.content: Distribute to every term inside parentheses.

items.title: Dividing by zero
items.content: Never divide by a coefficient that may be zero without considering that case.

keyTakeaways: A variable represents a number or quantity.
Only like terms can be combined.
The distributive property applies to every term inside parentheses.
A valid solution makes both sides of the original equation equal.

questionTypes: Form an equation from a statement
